items.title: Trump faults aides as Republican midterm prospects dim
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 17 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump is blaming senior aides and political operatives for a faltering midterm strategy, questioning campaign spending, faulting redistricting and second-guessing candidate choices as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress, said three people familiar with internal discussions.

Trump is not on the November 3 ballot but repeatedly tells supporters ​to pretend that he is, hoping to mobilize voters who might otherwise skip the election. He has embarked on a frenetic campaign schedule while largely avoiding acknowledging his own role in shaping ‌the strategy and how his unpopularity is weighing on Republican candidates in competitive races.

Much of the friction has centered on James Blair, the longtime aide who runs Trump's super PAC MAGA Inc., and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, who until now had largely escaped criticism. Trump has faulted Blair's handling of campaign funds, while some White House officials and allies have questioned Wiles' oversight of the political operation.

As Trump questions why campaign spending has failed to improve Republican polling numbers, his advisers are also blaming one another. Wiles has pointed to Blair, ​while Blair has faulted the White House legislative affairs team, one of the people said.

"What's really happening is a circular firing squad," the person said.

Opinion polls suggest Democrats will win the House of Representatives, while the ​Senate remains too close to call. Losing the House would hamper Trump's legislative agenda in the final two years of his term and give Democrats subpoena power to investigate ⁠his administration.

Trump defended Wiles on Friday, calling her "smart" and "tough" and saying she would remain in her job. "Susie is here, and she's going to be here for a long time," he said.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the sources' characterization, ​saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Wiles did not respond to a request for comment.

Trump has long sought to distance himself from political setbacks. He refused to accept his defeat in the ​2020 election and said ahead of the 2022 midterm results that he deserved "all the credit" if Republicans won but "should not be blamed at all" if they lost. More recently, he has reminded audiences that the president's party typically struggles in midterm elections.

But Trump helped devise and drive some of the strategies he is now questioning, including the redistricting effort and candidate choices shaped by his personal loyalties or grievances. His approval rating is at the lowest point of his presidency, weighed down by voter concern over high prices and dissatisfaction with the ​Iran war.

Trump's frustrations with his political team spilled into public view after Blair and Chris LaCivita, who co-managed Trump's 2024 campaign, traveled in early October to Republika Srpska, a self-governing region of Bosnia. The New York Times reported the ​men received substantial payments to advise the regional government ahead of local elections.

Trump distanced himself from both men, describing them as "outside consultants" in an October 7 Truth Social post and warning that if he found a conflict of interest, he would "terminate them, immediately!"

Senior White ‌House officials questioned ⁠why Blair was taking on lucrative work overseas when he was supposed to be overseeing the final stretch of the Republican campaign, three people said.

One person said Wiles approved the trip without informing Trump, raising questions about how closely she was overseeing his political advisers.

For Trump, the larger concern is that Blair's outside work has distracted him from his political responsibilities, two people said.

In a statement, Blair said: "All of this mudslinging is ridiculous, and counterproductive. President Trump and me are focused on helping Republicans win in November. Every other Republican should be doing the same."

In a separate statement, LaCivita said: "President Trump and his team are and always have been focused on the midterms. That's demonstrated through the money, message and motivation that ​the president is bringing on the road and all year. ​Sniping from unnamed cowards who've never been in a ⁠fight is not worth responding to."

With Trump asking why Republican polling in pivotal races has not improved despite MAGA Inc.'s campaign spending, which public records put at $200 million so far, it remains unclear whether he will approve more spending before the election, one of the sources said.

Trump also has pressed political aides and advisers in the past ​week to explain why the redistricting effort he personally pushed has failed to deliver more clear-cut Republican gains, two sources said.

Texas is a particular concern. Republicans redrew the ​state's congressional map to gain seats, ⁠but the strategy relies in part on Hispanic voters turning out as they did for the 2024 election. Opinion polls suggest that support may be difficult to replicate amid concerns about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. Some Republicans fear the new boundaries could backfire, leaving incumbents more vulnerable instead of giving the party an advantage.

"The redistricting diced up the Trump voters too much," one of the sources said.

Trump had said Blair was expected to return to the White House after ⁠the midterms, describing ​his departure as a "short leave of absence." But two sources said his return was now unlikely. "He's not coming back. That is not happening," one ​of them said.

It was less clear how things would play out for Wiles, who played a central role in Trump's 2024 victory and has been credited by Trump allies and aides with bringing greater discipline to his White House in his second term.

Trump "may be annoyed at certain things but ​she has effectively kept that machine going," a fourth source close to the White House said.

items.title: Trump threatens California officials with imprisonment over stance on mail ballots
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Friday warned ​Los Angeles County and California election officials they could be liable as abettors of a federal ‌crime if they count mail ballots returned by more than 20,000 people the Trump administration says are probably noncitizens.

The warning to the Los Angeles County Assistant Counsel Peter Bollinger came less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections and days after the department gave California 48 ​hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued ​California to block the state from counting the ballots.

"Noncitizen voting in a federal election is ⁠a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, ​wrote in a letter released on Friday. McCotter called on the county and California's secretary of state to reconsider their refusal ​to take steps that the Trump administration argues are needed to deter voter fraud.

US President Donald Trump shared the letter on Truth Social with the comment: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County ​Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan were copied on McCotter's letter.

The county's counsel office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Weber's ​office referred Reuters to an earlier statement in which she said the Justice Department's attempts to "unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter ‌data and ⁠purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."

An earlier letter that McCotter sent on Tuesday to Weber and Logan said the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" that were sent mail-in ballots from California.

Los Angeles County Counsel ​Dawyn R. Harrison said on ​Thursday the county cannot ⁠comply with the Justice Department's requests because the Trump administration did not explain how the list was made. Friday's letter from McCotter said the Justice Department used "internal immigration records" and ​data matching.

In July, Trump said his administration had uncovered evidence of more than 275,000 non-citizens registered ​to vote, ⁠but it was not clear how many had actually voted.

In some previous cases, systems intended to verify citizenship have mistakenly flagged some naturalized US citizens as noncitizens. Studies have found that noncitizens casting actual ballots is exceedingly uncommon.

Since July, the Justice Department ⁠has ramped up ​prosecutions of people accused of illegally voting while not holding US citizenship. ​The White House has also pushed federal agencies to accelerate their review of at least 47 state voter rolls obtained by the Department of Homeland Security, ​according to an internal email seen by Reuters.

items.title: Trump mocks popularity of the name Mohammad, common among Muslims
items.content_html:
DALTON, Georgia, Oct 16 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump made a joke about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world ​as he mocked Iran's presidency during a campaign speech on Friday.

"You ‌know, if you're in doubt about somebody's name from the Middle East, just say 'Mohammad,'" Trump told a crowd in Dalton, Georgia. "You have about a 65% chance. 'Hello, Mohammad.' I've done it ​for years now. I've never been wrong."

Mohammad is one of the most ​common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after ⁠the Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam.

Trump made the comment as he ​was discussing Iran during a rally in a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport ​in Georgia, where he campaigned for Republican political candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

"Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president," Trump said, then pretended to ​ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. Masoud Pezeshkian ​has been president of Iran since 2024.

The Georgia crowd gave the joke a muted response.

Rights advocates ‌and ⁠Muslim advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized Trump for rhetoric that they say demonizes and mocks Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities.

He has escalated such rhetoric during the midterm campaign season, particularly against Somali and Muslim Americans including Muslim Democratic US Senate ​candidate Abdul El-Sayed ​and Representative Ilhan ⁠Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who came to the US as a Somali refugee.

Trump repeated his vow that Iran would never ​get a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States ​and Israel ⁠launched a war on Tehran aimed in part at crippling its nuclear program.

An annual report by the Council on American Islamic Relations released earlier this year attributed rising ⁠Islamophobia ​in the US in part to Trump's crackdown ​on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term.

items.title: Teacher and armed parent teamed up to stop Oregon school shooter, police say
items.content_html:
BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A 16-year-old boy who shot and killed a teacher and three children in an Oregon special-needs classroom was ​stopped by another teacher who tackled him and an armed father who fatally shot him, officials said on Friday.

Their actions on Thursday saved other lives, the local police ‌chief told a press conference.

A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, police released new details of the scene at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where three schoolchildren aged 5, 8 and 11 were killed along with 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.

A 7-year-old was wounded and listed in serious but stable condition, and another teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said.

The unidentified teacher who stopped the shooter on Thursday threw her ​phone at him, tackled and fought him. A 36-year-old father of two students then rushed in with a legal .40-caliber pistol and fired at the suspect multiple times, killing him just before ​police arrived.

This teacher, who was not injured, "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, at times choking back emotion, told a press ⁠conference.

"The teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism," he said, without identifying her.

Kenda Freeman told the New York Times that her son Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters ​attend the school, killed the shooter, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.

"He is not seeking recognition but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first ​responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said, adding that he asked for privacy and did not want to speak to the media.

The shooting traumatized much of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, including 9-year-old fourth-grader Kalani Journeigh and her classmates, who heard the gunshots from a nearby classroom.

"All of us were screaming and we were all, like, really scared," Kalani told Reuters, adding that ​she feared, "We might die."

"My heart was beating really fast and after the couple of gunshots that we heard, it just stopped and we never heard it again," she said.

A friend of hers was going ​to get therapy, she said, because "that was really traumatizing to her."

Officials identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a 16-year-old former special-needs student at the school who was armed with a shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds ‌in the classroom ⁠and had another 44 rounds on him, police said.

Police were trying to determine what motivated the shooter and how he obtained a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun, Krantz said.

"Everyone wants to know why, including us," the police chief said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it."

Just before the shooting, the assailant was seen throwing his weapon over the school fence and then climbing after it onto school grounds. The driver of a truck passing by verbally confronted the boy, who opened fire on the vehicle.

The assailant shot through locked glass doors and stormed a class of mixed-grade special-needs students. Police arrived ​within three minutes of the first call, and the ​shooter was already dead, Krantz said.

People in ⁠Bend gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles outside yellow-crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene.

"Thank God for that father," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears. "He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should go out ​for him because he has a lot on his mind today."

The family of the slain teacher, Lambert, said working at Silver Rail was a "dream job" ​for her.

"She always fought ⁠for the underdog and those with special needs," the family said in a statement that was read aloud at Friday's news conference.

Lambert's family also praised Giamanco and expressed gratitude to him.

"We think he is a hero," the family said, according to the statement.

US school shootings have become more frequent in recent years. Since the start of this year, 118 people have been wounded or killed in 149 incidents involving a gun fired or brandished ⁠in a school, ​or gunshots striking school property, according to the K-12 School Shooting Database, a nonprofit online tracker.

A separate online database, the ​Gun Violence Archive, has recorded 371 mass shootings since January 2026, defining mass shootings as four or more people being struck by gunfire, not including the shooter. Three of those, including the Bend incident, occurred in public schools, the archive said.

items.title: US annual budget gap hits nearly $2 trillion, largest in 5 years
items.content_html:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - The US budget deficit rose by $217 billion to nearly $2 trillion in the ‌2026 fiscal year, fueled in part by tariff refunds and record spending to service the nation's more than $40 trillion in debt, marking the largest budget shortfall in five years, Treasury Department figures showed on Friday.

Continued increases in ​spending for social benefits programs like Social Security and Medicare and a $48 billion jump ​in defense spending also factored into the increase.

The $1.99 trillion deficit for the year ⁠ended September 30, the first full budget year of President Donald Trump's second term, was up from $1.78 ​trillion in fiscal 2025. It was the largest shortfall since fiscal 2021's $2.77 trillion budget gap, then ​fueled by COVID-19 pandemic relief spending, and is the third-largest annual deficit ever.

Total receipts for fiscal 2026 were a record $5.40 trillion, up $169 billion, or 3%, from the $5.24 trillion in fiscal 2025. Fiscal 2026 outlays also were a ​record at $7.40 trillion, up $386 billion, or 6%, from the $7.01 trillion in the prior fiscal year.

Debt-service outlays ​totaled a record $1.36 trillion, climbing by $144 billion, or 12%, a spending category now eclipsed only by Social Security ‌and ⁠the combined outlays for Medicare and Medicaid. Total US debt breached the $40 trillion milestone about two months ago.

Another driver of the widening shortfall was a $22 billion drop in net tariff receipts following a Supreme Court ruling this year negating a large portion of the tariffs Trump had imposed during ​his first year in ​office. That triggered $145 billion ⁠of tariff refunds over this year, resulting in an 11% decline in net tariff income to about $173 billion.

Defense spending for the year rose by ​6% to $917 billion. A US Treasury official said it was not clear ​how much ⁠of the increase could be attributed to the war Trump and Israel started against Iran earlier this year.

The Treasury official said the department calculated an estimated deficit-to-GDP ratio of 6.2% for fiscal 2026, but declined ⁠to say ​what GDP estimate was used. This figure compares to ​an actual 5.8% deficit-to-GDP ratio for fiscal 2025.

For the 2026 fiscal year's final month of September, the Treasury reported a ​deficit of $27 billion versus a $198 billion surplus a year earlier.

items.title: Actor Selma Blair did not intend harm on flight, spokesperson says
items.content_html:
LOS ANGELES, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A representative for Selma Blair, who was arrested this week and charged with assault for actions ​on a US Delta Air Lines flight, said on Friday the ‌actor did not intend to harm anyone or open an aircraft door.

A statement issued by her publicist repeated comments from earlier this week that Blair, who has ​multiple sclerosis, suffered a medical emergency on the flight from Los ​Angeles to New York. Blair did not try to open ⁠a door on the plane as some media outlets reported, the statement ​said.

"There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma ​did not intend to harm anyone," the statement said.

Blair pleaded not guilty on Monday to charges of assaulting a police officer involved in her arrest at New York's ​John F. Kennedy Airport and a nurse at the hospital where she ​was taken afterward.

Police met the plane when it landed after reports of a "physically abusive ‌passenger" ⁠who was identified as Blair, according to a statement from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey's police department. Two flight attendants reported injuries and one of them was taken to a hospital, police said.

Blair, ​54, is known ​for roles in "Cruel ⁠Intentions" and "Hellboy." She has spoken publicly about being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018.

The statement by Blair's representative ​said Blair has a neurological condition known as pseudobulbar ​affect, "which bears ⁠directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her."

"There is much more to this story than has been reported, and ⁠we ask ​to consider the entirety of the facts ​before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion," ​Blair's representatives said.

items.title: US military weighs use of ‘mother of all bombs’ in potential future strikes on Iran, CNN says
items.content_html:
Oct 15 (Reuters) - The US military has developed strike plans ​that could include using ‌the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known ​as the "mother of ​all bombs", against Iranian energy ⁠infrastructure and nuclear sites ​if President Donald Trump ​orders renewed combat operations, CNN reported on Thursday citing US ​officials familiar with the ​matter.

The potential deployment of the largest ‌non-nuclear ⁠bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the ​conflict, ​although ⁠officials familiar with military planning discussions ​told CNN questions remain ​over ⁠its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.

Reuters could ⁠not ​immediately verify the ​report.

items.title: Hacker gets data on millions of California students, state education department says
items.content_html:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - The California Department of Education said on Friday a hacker accessed the data of millions of students, including names, birth dates, addresses and ​disability status, by exploiting the system of a non-profit contractor that ‌works with the state.

The hacker accessed the data of "all students enrolled in the three previous school years," the department said. More than 5.7 million students were enrolled in California ​during the 2025-2026 school year, according to the department.

The non-profit, Educational Testing ​Service, on Friday began notifying students and their families of ⁠the breach, which was identified late last month but found to have ​been ongoing since May, the education department said.

The non-profit identified the breach involving ​a secure file transfer protocol site on September 25 and began an investigation, according to the California agency.

"The investigation determined that an unauthorized party used a compromised login credential to ​access the site and copy files containing California student information at various ​times between May 22 and September 18, 2026," the education department said.

Educational Testing Service has ‌not ⁠found that any of the information has been made public so far, the education department said, adding that Social Security numbers and sensitive financial information were not accessed.

In an October 2 letter to county and district school officials, the ​California agency said ​the testing service ⁠had stopped "normal enrollment data processing."

"The CDE is actively working to minimize disruption and resume affected assessment activities in a ​timely manner," the department said.

In California, Educational Testing Service administers ​statewide assessments ⁠including those for English language proficiency.

"We have implemented additional safeguards, including enhanced monitoring, strengthened access controls, and further third-party review of our security practices," Educational Testing ⁠Service said ​in a statement to Reuters. "Our priority remains the ​students, families and educators we serve and safeguarding the assessment programs we deliver for our clients ​and partners globally."

items.title: US lifts curbs on Mexican airlines after aviation dispute
items.content_html:
MEXICO CITY, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Mexican airlines will be able to launch new flights to the US from Mexico City's two international airports after the US Department of ​Transportation lifted restrictions imposed over aviation disputes between the two countries, Mexico's government ‌said on Friday.

The decision allows airlines to establish routes to the US from Mexico City's Felipe Angeles International Airport (AIFA) and Benito Juarez International Airport, according to a statement from the ministries of foreign affairs and communications and ​transportation.

The US Department of Transportation said the move reflected steps taken by Mexico to ​address concerns over its compliance with a 2015 bilateral air transport agreement.

The ⁠department said it would continue to require Mexican carriers to file schedules for flights to ​and from the US and obtain approval to operate services using large aircraft.

A US official ​said two other orders related to the dispute remain in place and that Washington would closely monitor Mexico's compliance with its commitments.

The official said the decision was separate from an ongoing Federal Aviation Administration review ​of Mexico's aviation oversight efforts conducted in August.

The FAA restored Mexico's top air safety ​rating in September 2023, allowing Mexican airlines to expand existing US routes and launch new services. Mexico had ‌been downgraded ⁠in May 2021 after the US regulator found the country did not meet international aviation safety standards.

The downgrade was a major blow to Mexican carriers, as US airlines were able to scoop up market share.

In May, opens new tab, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the Mexican government had agreed to improve ​aviation access to Mexico ​City.

President Donald Trump's administration had ⁠reached an agreement with Mexico on a plan to address US concerns over its compliance with a 2015 air transport agreement between the ​two countries, Duffy said.

In October last year, the US froze the expansion ​of Mexican ⁠airlines' passenger and cargo services from the two airports, alleging Mexico had not complied with the bilateral aviation agreement since 2022, when it rescinded slots held by US passenger airlines and forced US ⁠all-cargo carriers ​to relocate operations.

Mexican airlines welcomed Friday's decision. Carriers Viva and Aeromexico (AERO.MX), opens new tab said it ​would strengthen air connectivity between the two countries.

items.title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI engineer over covert recording device, DOJ says
items.content_html:
Oct 13 (Reuters) - US federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording ‌device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday.

The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice ​Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name did not elicit a response, and it ​was not immediately clear who his lawyer was.

OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the ⁠back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to the department.

The thumb-sized ​device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about ​September 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan's personal bag.

OpenAI said in a post, opens new tab on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins.

The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording ​devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating ​model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the company said.

OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi ‌embassy in ⁠the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

"Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through September 16, according to the FBI complaint. He has been a legal permanent ​resident of the US since September ​2020.

If convicted, Alfozan faces up to ⁠five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release.

A LinkedIn profile showed that Alfozan studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, ​it said.

Reuters could not independently verify the details mentioned in his LinkedIn profile.

Separately, the Information reported, opens new tab that OpenAI was ​in early talks ⁠to acquire Trail of Bits, a startup that identifies and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software. The talks were ongoing and could fall apart, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.

OpenAI and Trail of Bits did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers ⁠after an investigation ​found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information.

The researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek ​Korbak and Mikita Balesni, had published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture in which researchers could ​raise safety concerns.

items.title: Anthropic to add US voting information to Claude before midterms
items.content_html:
Oct 14 (Reuters) - (This Oct 14 story has been corrected to say that chats about whom or what to vote for accounted for 0.01% of US conversations, not requests for recommendations on how to vote, in paragraph 7.)

Anthropic said on Wednesday it would add official US voting information from nonprofit Democracy Works and ​election results to its Claude AI chatbot ​later this month, ahead of the November midterms.

The ⁠AI company said its goal was to position ​Claude as a useful tool for political conversations, while ​preventing election-related abuse.

"Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy or social issues account for about 5.75% of all ​conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our ​consumer app," the company said in a statement, citing analysis of ‌250,000 ⁠US conversations.

The move comes as AI companies increasingly position chatbots as sources of news and information, potentially helping Anthropic draw more users during the election cycle.

About ​0.51% of ​Claude conversations ⁠are specifically about elections or voting, Anthropic said, adding that it expects political ​and election-related queries to rise as election ​day ⁠approaches.

Later this month, US users seeking voting logistics will receive answers drawn directly from Democracy Works' database of ⁠state ​and local election sources.

Anthropic said chats on ​whom or what to vote for were 0.01% of U.S. conversations.

items.title: Trump shuts down Hegseth plan to livestream military execution
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump scrapped plans to livestream the execution of the former ​Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, overruling Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Thursday after the proposal drew opposition ‌from Republicans, religious leaders and the public.

The reversal ended a plan to broadcast Nidal Hasan’s December 3 firing-squad execution. It also marked a rare public disagreement between Trump and one of the president’s closest allies, although the Pentagon said the two were “completely aligned.”

Hegseth had announced plans to livestream the execution at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, the ​site of Hasan's 2009 attack. No other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions.

Trump and his advisers had been unaware ​of the livestream plan, said a White House official speaking on condition of anonymity.

"I think streaming the execution for all ⁠to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very ​good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote in a social media ​post. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."

The families of Hasan's victims will be able to view the execution in person if they so choose, as is standard at US executions.

Some of Trump's fellow Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, as well as religious leaders had expressed everything from doubts to outright condemnation ​of the Pentagon's livestream plan.

Opinion polls showed a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming it. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members ​of the US armed forces, also raised objections, while Pope Leo condemned capital punishment in all its forms.

An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment, ‌and it ⁠was unclear if the scheduled December 3 execution date would be delayed by legal challenges.

It was Trump's first major public split with Hegseth, a Trump ally. But it was unclear whether the split would politically imperil Hegseth given their strong ties.

In a statement, the Pentagon said Trump spoke with Hegseth about the decision before announcing it on Truth Social.

"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said ​in a statement.

Capital punishment in the ​US already was facing renewed scrutiny ⁠after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived two lethal injections in a failed execution attempt by Tennessee last month that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalization.

A military jury convicted Hasan, a former US ​Army psychiatrist, of premeditated murder for fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers and wounding 32 others in a medical ​facility at the vast ⁠base. Law enforcement shot Hasan during his rampage, paralyzing him from the waist down, and he now uses a wheelchair.

Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that "there's serious consequences for these types of things."

Midterm elections on November 3 will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress as ⁠voters increasingly ​register disapproval of Trump's policies in opinion polls.

Senator John Curtis, a Republican representing Utah, called ​the cancellation "the right move" in a statement.

US Representative Richard Neal, a Democrat from Massachusetts, called the original plan "a profound failure of moral judgment and basic human decency."

items.title: On the campaign trail, JB Pritzker courts farmers like he's running for president
items.content_html:
CHICAGO, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The town of Shirley, Illinois, population 135, is an unlikely place for a campaign stop.

Yet billionaire Democrat JB Pritzker traveled there to spar with his opponent in his bid for a third term as governor of the state in the November midterms. At Funk Farms, ​a 200-year-old corn, soybean and livestock operation there that was once represented by young lawyer and future president Abraham Lincoln, he extolled the virtues of farming.

“Agriculture drives an enormous part of Illinois' economy. We've got to do ‌all we can to weather the storm and get Washington to take a different course,” Pritzker said at the August event.

Pritzker's visits to farms across Illinois reflect a broader Democratic effort to capitalize on farmer frustration over lost export markets and rising costs tied to President Donald Trump's tariffs and war with Iran. But analysts see his trips as largely an effort to cultivate a rural profile before a possible 2028 run for the White House, given he does not need farmers to win in November.

A Republican has not won statewide office in Illinois since 2014, and most political forecasters give Pritzker a solid lead over Republican candidate Darren ​Bailey, a third-generation soybean farmer and former state lawmaker whom he defeated by about 12 percentage points in 2022.

Pritzker, an heir to the Hyatt hotels fortune, also boasts a campaign war chest that dwarfs Bailey's. It was recently replenished with $65 million ​of his own money.

“He’s auditioning,” said Brian J. Gaines, a political science professor at the University of Illinois. “He’s not banking on Illinois farmers but if he finds something that works, he’s going to ⁠keep it in his pocket because he’s thinking about the presidential contest to come.”

Pritzker refused to be drawn in on whether he plans to run for president in 2028, saying Democrats need to focus on winning in the midterms first. "Anybody that's focused on anything beyond ​November 3rd, as far as I'm concerned, is getting it wrong," he said in an interview.

This month, Pritzker toured Halpin Farms, a family grain and cattle operation about 70 miles (113 km) southwest of Chicago, promoting a pilot program of low-interest state loans to build grain silos. ​He talked about how agriculture remained a critical industry in Illinois, even as he looks to quantum computing and advanced manufacturing to drive economic growth in the state.

"Family farms are going bankrupt. It's near impossible to make a profit now because of the high price of diesel, because of the war in Iran, and because of the trade wars that are causing the farmers not to be able to sell their goods abroad," Pritzker told Reuters. "Right now, we need to make sure our farmers stay alive and stay in business."

Farmers in Illinois have struggled as Trump's trade wars cut off markets for US soybeans ​and the US-Israeli war with Iran led to soaring fuel and fertilizer prices, though the White House says it has "strengthened the farm safety net."

If Pritzker can demonstrate that he can appeal to a traditionally conservative bloc like farmers, Gaines said, it could help him distinguish ​himself from Democrats like former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Governor Gavin Newsom, potential contenders with considerably less credibility in the farm belt.

Pritzker is not the only Democrat courting that strategy.

This week, US Representative Ro Khanna, a California Democrat who represents Silicon Valley, flew to rural Georgia to highlight the impact ‌of tariffs and ⁠higher production costs while former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg traveled to rural Virginia to rally for congressional candidates there. Rahm Emanuel, a former Chicago mayor and White House chief of staff for former President Barack Obama, has been up and down the Midwestern Corn Belt and in the Deep South in recent months to address what he calls "healthcare deserts" hit by Trump administration policies.

"There's a political opportunity" for Democrats in rural areas, Emanuel told Reuters.

Bailey acknowledges that the Republican administration's trade policies and war in Iran have hurt farmers.

"I think everyone would agree that we're ready for the conflict in Iran to be over with, and would have hoped that these tariffs would have ended a long time ago," he said.

But Bailey said that Pritzker’s focus on Trump missed the point – that slashing property taxes and doing away with an estate ​tax would help farmers much more than “pandering,” as would embracing some ​of the austerity measures that farmers have undertaken to survive ⁠high costs.

The Trump administration is expected to send more than $50 billion to farmers this year, the second-largest relief package in US history. Yet many farmers say the checks don't make up for the high input costs.

"We're getting beat up," said John Bartman, 48, a corn and soybean farmer in Marengo, Illinois, adding that "a bailout doesn't make us whole. It helps the banks out more than the farmer."

Bartman, ​who plans to vote for Pritzker, said he thinks farmers will value the governor's efforts to salvage important trade relationships.

In August, Pritzker signed an agreement with Indonesia to expand agricultural trade with ​the fourth-largest market for US soybeans. He previously led ⁠trade missions to Canada and Japan in 2024. And in April 2025, as the Trump administration imposed tariffs on imports from most trading partners on what it called "Liberation Day," Pritzker was in Mexico City to promote Illinois corn.

That visit to Mexico - the top market for US corn - landed a $55 million manufacturing deal, but did not bag new deals to buy Illinois corn.

"As a governor, there's only so much you can do about federal policy," Pritzker said.

The speculation of a presidential run has soared since last year, when Trump launched an aggressive deportation campaign in the Chicago area, briefly ⁠deploying the National Guard.

Pritzker ​denounced the campaign as federal overreach, comparing the immigration raids in Chicago to the antisemitic pogroms his Ukrainian ancestors escaped from.

Pritzker has also used Trump's mockery ​of his weight as a foil, speaking candidly about his struggles with overeating and writing about his GLP-1 journey on Substack.

At the Illinois State Fair in August, he praised deep-fried treats and later that month helped Chicago set a record for most people taking a shot of Malort at the same time, swigging the intensely bitter ​liqueur straight from the bottle.

Standing in front of a row of Black Angus cows at Halpin Farms, he joked, "these are my people. I've certainly eaten enough of them."

items.title: Nvidia, Apple each gave $25 million for Trump's ballroom, Washington Post reports
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Nvidia (NVDA.O), opens new tab and Apple (AAPL.O), opens new tab each committed $25 million for US President Donald Trump's planned White House ballroom, according to a Washington Post report on Thursday that showed $333 million in private donations ​for the project.

The Adelson family, longtime financial supporters of Trump and his Republican Party, committed $25 million as well, as ‌did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network, the report added.

The president himself is not on the list, according to the Post.

Reuters has not verified the report. The White House said it would not release information about the donors, who spokesman Davis Ingle said "represent a wide array of great American companies."

"The same critics ​who are alleging fake conflicts of interests would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue ​renovations," Ingle told Reuters.

Nvidia said it was proud to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves ⁠Americans. "As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," a spokesperson said.

Apple declined to ​comment.

The scale of the ballroom project and the administration’s handling of fundraising and disclosures have drawn criticism from watchdog groups and legal experts, who ​say they raise questions about transparency, donor influence and adherence to longstanding ethics and oversight norms.

"The secrecy is a huge problem," said Eric Petry of the Brennan Center for Justice. "When people with business before the government can give millions to the president's pet project, and the public can't see who or how much, there's ​no way to tell whether they're buying access or favors."

Federal contractors including Lockheed Martin Corp, Microsoft Corp and Palantir Technologies Inc all gave $10 ​million, the Post reported. The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Trump initially said he and wealthy donors would pay for the ‌estimated $400 million ⁠project, but he later unsuccessfully sought $1 billion from Congress for an underground bunker and security features to harden the facility.

The Post reported that the "vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government" and that half the total came from companies or executives of firms that have had federal government contracts in Trump's second White House term.

The planned ballroom is among several projects Trump ​is pursuing in his efforts to ​remake Washington with sweeping, unilateral changes ⁠that his opponents have challenged in court and called a power grab.

The US Supreme Court, in a 5-4 ruling in August, allowed Trump to continue construction of the ballroom while he challenges a judicial order that ​would halt much of the development. In a dissent, Chief Justice John Roberts said the project was "likely ​unlawful."

The ballroom, which ⁠Trump has said will seat 1,000 guests, has faced public backlash. Preservationists and opponents say Trump exceeded his authority by demolishing the historic East Wing, which housed the first lady's offices and the White House movie theater, to make room for the structure.

Trump says a planned 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) White House ballroom ⁠will include ​bomb shelters, medical facilities, defenses against drones and missiles and other security features. Confronted ​with criticism of the project, his administration now says the facility is needed for national security, an argument the president has also made about a proposed triumphal arch.

items.title: US Treasury pushes global partners to rename AI as 'super intelligence'
items.content_html:
BANGKOK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The United States wants its global partners to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," convinced that the new moniker better reflects the emerging technology, a top ​US Treasury official told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.

Treasury Undersecretary for International ‌Affairs Erin Browne said Washington was in negotiations with other shareholders of the International Monetary Fund about using the new term in a statement being drafted by the fund's steering committee, the International Monetary and ​Financial Committee.

US President Donald Trump last month directed US government agencies to use ​the words "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" when referring to the technology.

Browne said the ⁠United States, which holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, ​wanted the change to take hold internationally as well.

"President Trump has been really clear on this, ​and he's, you know, using the term SI, and I think it's a clear priority for the US to use that term, and we think that more appropriately encapsulates the technology at hand," Browne said.

She ​declined to comment on whether Washington would refuse to sign off on the statement unless ​the switch was made.

"We're still in the middle of negotiations on that statement, so I'm not going ‌to, you ⁠know, sort of run ahead of that," she said.

A source familiar with the matter said US officials had suggested during meetings on the IMFC statement that they would insist on the new language, raising eyebrows among some other IMFC members.

If Washington withholds its support for a ​consensus statement, the current ​IMFC chair, Saudi ⁠Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, could still issue a so-called chair's statement summarizing the views of the members.

One possibility might involve skipping a mention ​of SI or AI and focusing on "new technology" instead, the source ​said.

The IMFC ⁠will hold a news conference and release any agreed statement led by Al-Jadaan and IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday.

"We see this as a driving force behind American growth and global ⁠growth," Browne ​said.

"Many countries are looking to the US to set ​the standards, as well as to set the path forward for SI development and how that can really enhance ​and boost growth and productivity on a global basis."

items.title: Trump says he wants death penalty for anyone who kills a firefighter
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - US President ​Donald Trump said ​on Thursday he wants the ⁠death penalty for ​anyone who kills a ​firefighter.

Trump, who previously has called for the death penalty for ​anyone found guilty ​of killing a police officer, made ‌the ⁠comment during a White House Rose Garden lunch honoring firefighter organizations.

Trump ​said he ​had ⁠directed the Justice Department to seek ​the death penalty ​in ⁠such cases, specifically "anybody that murders a firefighter going ⁠up ​a ladder."

items.title: Trump's AI task force to meet Thursday, FTC spokesperson says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's new government task force on ​AI is scheduled to meet on Thursday, a ‌Federal Trade Commission spokesperson said, as pressure builds on Washington to confront the risks posed by the rapidly ​advancing technology.

The task force is expected to ​help shape the administration's approach to AI ⁠at a pivotal moment for public opinion ​of the technology. Public uneasiness with AI, ​and the small group of executives driving its development, has risen in recent months. Most American voters think ​Trump's administration and Congress are not taking ​the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government ‌to ⁠write new regulations for the technology, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published October 7.

Trump has dubbed the group the Super Intelligence Task Force, ​using his preferred ​term for ⁠artificial intelligence. It is led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, with ​Office of Personnel Management Director Scott ​Kupor, FTC Chairman ⁠Andrew Ferguson and Defense Department technology lead Emil Michael.

Kupor told Reuters last week that he expects ⁠the ​group to release a charter ​outlining its goals and responsibilities after its first full committee ​meeting.

items.title: FBI, US Postal Service investigate suspicious mailings to election officials, lawmakers
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The FBI and US Postal Service's law enforcement arm said on Thursday ​they were investigating suspicious mailings, including some sent to state election officials and lawmakers' offices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

The ‌FBI said some of the letters contained an unknown substance.

The investigation come less than three weeks before the midterms, which will determine control of the US Congress, as the Postal Service prepares to handle millions of mailed ballots.

Spokespeople for Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, and Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, all said the US ​Postal Service intercepted letters containing a suspicious substance mailed to their offices.

"This incident is a stark reminder of the very real dangers facing ​those who serve the public and who help administer our elections," Padilla said in a statement.

The US House of ⁠Representatives sergeant at arms, the House's chief law enforcement officer, told staff in an email seen by Reuters that some public officials had received letters ​containing suspicious white powder substances.

Brendan Donahue, a deputy chief inspector with the US Postal Inspection Service, said some suspicious letters had been intercepted and that an ​investigation was ongoing.

"We are committed to protecting our nation's election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable," Donahue told reporters.

The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said late on Wednesday a series of suspicious letters was sent to state election offices. ​Letters bound for several state election offices were intercepted before they were delivered, including in Pennsylvania, Ohio and Idaho.

The Wisconsin Elections Commission said on Thursday ​it received a suspicious letter with an unidentified powdery substance that was deemed not hazardous. "Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us,” said Meagan Wolfe, the ‌state’s chief ⁠election official.

An email to Senate staff said suspicious letters could have postmarks that do not match the return address and included an image of an envelope with a return address labeled "DSA" and a New York City address.

Earlier on Thursday, US Postmaster General David Steiner said USPS was "absolutely ready" to handle millions of ballots for the midterm elections.

USPS said this month it would take "extraordinary measures" for the 2026 election, including extending hours at some ​retail locations and expediting handling, extra deliveries ​and special pickups of ballots.

On ⁠September 14, the US Supreme Court declined to let USPS enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump's effort to restrict voting by mail. USPS said it would not enforce the rule under the ​order.

The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail ​voting.

In 2024, USPS delivered ⁠99.2 million ballots to and from voters in the presidential election. About 30% of votes were cast by mail in the November 2024 presidential election, down from 46% in 2020.

Trump's fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according to ⁠various surveys, ​so restricting them could benefit Republicans.

Under the rule that was blocked, states would have had ​to provide lists of mail-ballot recipients to USPS and use agency-approved outbound and return ballot mail envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes. The Postal Service could then have refused to send out ballots ​that did not comply or were associated with voters not appearing on the lists.

items.title: NEWSLETTER: 13 stops, 11 states. Where's Trump's cost-of-living message?
items.content_html:
Oct 15 (Reuters) - On two recent reporting trips to Texas, I spoke to supporters of President Donald Trump who said they were frustrated by rising costs but still confident that he can turn the economy around. Yet, less than three weeks before the midterms, Trump is saying little about inflation or how he plans to lower prices. At recent rallies, he has ​instead attacked political opponents, waxed nostalgic about his first term and taken extended detours into personal grievances.

Trump has spent more than ‌16 hours speaking at 13 appearances across 11 states since October 1, by my rough count. But many of the headlines generated by those appearances have had little to do with the cost of living.

All 13 appearances aimed to boost Republican turnout ahead of the November 3 midterms. Trump talks about the economy, but rarely for long or in much detail. He touts manufacturing investments, recalls cheaper gas before the Iran war, asserts gas prices were ​higher under President Joe Biden and promises they will fall once the war ends. In Montana, he dismissed concerns that tariffs fuel inflation, insisting the country has "very little ​inflation," although the latest government data showed it rising to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August. He has also pledged $5,000 payouts to all ⁠American adults if Republicans win. But the scattered remarks don't add up to a clear affordability message.

Democrats have attacked Trump over rising costs, but they, too, have struggled to offer voters a ​clear economic message.

At five recent rallies, Trump repeated a story about spotting gasoline at $1.85 or $1.95 a gallon during a January visit to Iowa. But fuel-price tracker GasBuddy found no regular gasoline that cheap ​among more than 2,000 stations it monitored that day. The statewide average was $2.57, according to auto association AAA. The anecdote illustrates how Trump's economic message can lean on memories rather than offer new solutions.

Even when he addresses the economy, the message often gets lost in his own digressions.

In Youngstown, Ohio, Trump went from announcing a submarine-component facility to admiring the jawline of US Senator Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican. In Syracuse, New York, he complained ​about not receiving the Nobel Peace Prize. In Tennessee, he suggested renaming an ocean after himself. His Texas rally with Senate candidate Ken Paxton made news for protesters, while in Alaska, he signed presidential ​pardons onstage.

There are exceptions. At a Baltimore-area shipyard, Trump announced a $3.7 billion private investment in submarine manufacturing, while a Texas factory visit highlighted jobs and tariffs. Both generated economic coverage. But unlike his sprawling rallies, those visits ‌were built around ⁠specific announcements.

The political backdrop is getting tougher for Republicans – recent polling has added to concerns about their ability to hold on to Congress.

With Republicans increasingly relying on Trump to rally their voters, his appearances have taken on greater importance. But they also mean the president, rather than the candidates themselves, often determines what gets talked about in the final weeks of the campaign.

He repeatedly tells supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, hoping to mobilize voters who might otherwise skip the midterms. In close races, that could matter.

But firing up the base is only part of the task. ​Republicans also need to attract voters unhappy with ​the economy who aren't committed to either ⁠party. They may never attend a Trump rally, but they'll see the headlines.

Special Report: In Trump’s pardons for public officials, Republicans win most of the mercy

Musk has spent $276 million on midterms to help Republicans retain control of Congress

Inside the booming market for US midterm election bets

Democratic midterm wins could bring scrutiny ​for Wall Street, crypto firms

Trump's effort to lower energy prices ahead of the midterms is creating friction with a close European ally. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called a US-Russia diesel deal a "very risky choice" on Wednesday, warning it could undermine efforts to pressure Moscow into ending its war in Ukraine. Trump ⁠has defended the arrangement, ​saying it would lower energy costs, but European leaders worry it could provide Russia with revenue while weakening sanctions.
